extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature; poets and creative writers interested in Sir Philip Sidney's 'Apology for Poetry' and its editorial commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative claims about poetry drawn from Sir Philip Sidney’s Apology for Poetry (with editorial footnotes), addressing poetry’s nature, kinds, aims, and stylistic cautions. Useful for assessing or composing poetry in a Renaissance-critical framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is the one creative art
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry is the one creative art." (footnote: "Poetry is the one creative art. Astronomers and others repeat what they find.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes poets as makers (creators) rather than mere reporters; implies criterion that poetry should invent or create imaginatively rather than simply replicate facts or observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets improve Nature
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should not merely copy nature but ennoble or surpass it — i.e., idealize, refine, and improve natural phenomena or human character in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry idealizes man
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of poetry's tasks is to present elevated or ideal forms of human behavior and character; effective poetry shapes exemplary or heightened versions of humanity for instruction or delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence is in the thought, not in the apparel of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its essence is in the thought, not in apparelling of verse." (footnote 22)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize idea, imagination, and meaning over mere verbal ornament, metre, or rhetorical dressing; substantive thought is the primary measure of poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry advances virtuous action
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry best advances the end of all earthly learning, virtuous action." (footnote 26)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats poetry as morally and pedagogically valuable — a key evaluative standard is whether the poem promotes virtue or ethical improvement more effectively than other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's advantage over Moral Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney claims poetry has greater persuasive force than abstract moral philosophy; criterion: poetry should move readers toward right action where philosophy may only instruct abstractly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's advantage over History
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its advantage herein over History." (footnote 28 and expanded in note 35: Aristotle — poetry deals with what might be, general truth; history deals with what has been, particulars.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its capacity to represent general truths (probable or necessary patterns of human behaviour) rather than merely recounting particular events; universality and generalizability are virtues in poetic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds and subdivisions of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry defined. Its kinds. a. Divine. b. Philosophical (which is perhaps too imitative). c. Poetry proper. § 3. Subdivisions of Poetry proper." (footnotes 16–21)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify poetic work by kind (divine, philosophical, poetry proper) and by its subdivisions; choose form and methods suited to the kind — e.g., beware that philosophical poetry may risk mere imitation rather than creative making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's sacred/prophetic status (and classical esteem)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Honoured by the Romans as Sacred and Prophetic." and references to Greeks calling poets 'Makers' (footnotes 9–11)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney presents poetry as occupying a high cultural and moral status — when composing or judging poetry, consider whether it aspires to the gravity/sacredness or prophetic insight that classical tradition attributes to poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on hackneyed common-places
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the rhetorical term 'common-place' (locus communis) and caution: "Frequent resort to the Polyanthea caused many a good quotation to be hackneyed; the term of rhetoric, 'a common-place,' came then to mean a good saying made familiar by incessant quoting..." (footnote 34)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overuse trite sayings or well-worn quotations; originality and freshness of expression are evaluative virtues; excessive recourse to commonplaces weakens poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Poet's Work: what poetry does for us
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Poet’s Work and Parts. § 1. WORK: What Poetry does for us." (footnote 24)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry instrumentally: assess poems by their contribution to human understanding, moral formation, memory, and delight — the poem’s social/intellectual function is a criterion of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mediocrity; strive for excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's line noted: "Neither men, gods, nor lettered columns have admitted mediocrity in poets." (footnote 33)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard that poets should aim beyond mediocrity; quality and excellence are non-negotiable expectations in poetic craft.
